brief.head: Why religion exists
brief.text: Consolation, explanation and codification: Amit Varma offered three reasons religion exists. {076-C04} Ajay Shah added that coherent bands of 150 believers won wars. {#bands}

brief.head: Seeker to columnist
brief.text: Raja Ram Mohan Roy began as a seeker, writing in Persian, Amit Varma said. Writing later in Bengali, he became something like a modern columnist, out to persuade. {076-S10}

brief.head: No cotton-wearers
brief.text: Worshipping Shiva or Vishnu once conferred no identity, the historian Manu Devadevan argues, any more than wearing cotton made anyone a “cotton wearer”. {076-C07}

brief.head: Freelance zeal
brief.text: The Industrial Revolution created the freelance missionary, Amit Varma said: anyone, even a shoemaker, could go out, and journals of their accounts sold in the hundreds of thousands. {076-S08}

brief.head: Prudes from abroad
brief.text: What passes for sanskari modesty, Amit Varma argued, is a Victorian import. William Jones’s translation drained the sensuality from the original *Shakuntala*. {076-S09}

thought.text: What happens when you write something down is that it becomes ossified.

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on a faith of many stories
lead.head: More Hinduisms than Hindus
body: Amit Varma opened with a disclaimer. He is a non-believer, he said, and has been for all his adult life. But Hinduism is “a river that runs through this space and through all of us”, and the simple stories told about it miss the point.

He named two. The first is nationalist: a glorious Hindu past, interrupted by foreign invaders, that must be revived as a Hindu rashtra. The second is academic, and Varma said he held it until recently: Hinduism as a recent construction, its name coined by a Britisher in the late 18th century, its Vedic version sold to the British by Brahmin interlocutors.
Both, he argued, are imposed from the top. Following the historian Manu Pillai, he offered a third view: “the name may be new, but the river was always there.” {076-C01}
Over the next hour and a quarter, with Ajay Shah asking the questions, he followed that river from the first humans to the present.
## Mixed from the start

Modern humans reached the subcontinent between 65,000 and 60,000 years ago, Varma said. Pastoralists from Iran settled at Mehrgarh about 7,000 years ago, and migrants from the steppes arrived around 2100 BCE, mostly men, who mixed with the locals.
Genetics, he said, can now date such arrivals where archaeology could not. “Now we don’t know whether they invaded or not, but there certainly was an Aryan migration.” {076-C02}
Even Sanskrit picked up sounds from languages already spoken here. “It itself is a khichdi,” Varma said. {076-S01}

In the Puranic period that followed, Brahmins without the power to impose their beliefs absorbed local gods instead of erasing them. Varma called it “a curation driven by spontaneous order”, a religion “forming itself from the bottom up”. {076-C05}
Shah compared it to language, which shifts a little every hundred kilometres.
## Borders drawn

Invasions from the north gave feuding sects their first sense of a common other. Colonialism sharpened it. Varma retold Pillai’s image of four squabbling brown-skinned men who feel united only when a white man attacks them all. {076-C09}
Europeans who could not grasp an open-source religion, Varma said, did what minds do with too much complexity: they made up a story, “which is possibly false”. {076-C10}
Indian responses followed. Raja Ram Mohan Roy’s genteel Brahmo Samaj pleased the British; Dayanand Saraswati’s Arya Samaj outlasted it. Bal Gangadhar Tilak took religion onto the streets.
Vinayak Savarkar then supplied a test of belonging: India had to be both your homeland and your holy land. “Hinduism is a subset of Hindutva,” Varma said, summing up Savarkar’s idea. {076-C11}
## What remains
Caste, Varma said, is a social evil, like sati, and it has to go. He is sceptical of top-down fixes. His hope lies in markets, where those who discriminate pay a price. {076-C12}

Shah predicted that prosperity would do its own work. Religiosity peaks in the middle, he said, and India, after the 1991 reforms, is there now. “In time secularisation will come for India as well.” {076-C13}

Varma ended with an appeal to English-speaking urban elites: don’t be condescending. He used to think there were as many Hinduisms as there are Hindus. Now, he said, he thinks there are more. {076-J07}
Read history, he urged, to understand how things came to be, while keeping your own values intact. {076-C16}

second.label: The open-source epics
second.head: Bengal drew the line
second.deck: Amit Varma on the Ramayana as a river, rewritten across regions and centuries
body: The Lakshman Rekha, today a metaphor for a line no one should cross, is not in Valmiki’s Ramayana. It first appears, Amit Varma said, in Krittivasa’s Bengali version, from around the 15th century. {#rekha}

Drawing on AK Ramanujan’s essay *300 Ramayanas*, Varma called the epics open source, rewritten at different times and places according to local customs. {076-R17} Surpanakha is ugly in Valmiki and beautiful in Kamban. In the Telugu version, Urmila sleeps for fourteen years, half for herself and half for Lakshman, so that he can stay awake.
Krittivasa also added the washerman who starts the gossip about Sita. Varma was not disturbed that there is no one book; he finds it “utterly wonderful”. {076-S03}

quote.text: you never step into the same river twice, so you never step into the same Ramayana twice, and that’s amazing.

second.caption: the open-source Ramayana

third.head: Nothing to teach them
body: Bartholomäus Ziegenbalg arrived with the usual missionary impulse: convert these people. Then he engaged, Amit Varma said, and found much wisdom in the later Vedas.

He wrote to his superiors that they had got it wrong. “There is nothing we have to teach them,” he wrote, as Varma told it. “The best of our learnings are mirrored somewhere or the other in their teachings.” {076-S07}
His superiors slapped him down. In effect, Varma said, they accused him of Stockholm syndrome, “though of course the term didn’t exist then”. {076-J04}

Manu Pillai records many such respectful dialogues and debates, Varma said, but they were a small minority in a shrill discourse, much as intelligent discourse is today. That age, he joked, also had its own Amit Varma and Ajay Shah, chatting civilly with British interlocutors. {076-J05}
third.caption: the missionary who changed his mind

p2.title: Contains multitudes
p2.deck: From the steppes to Savarkar, a tradition that grew from below and only later acquired borders

sections.label: The deep past
sections.head: Nomads through a narrow pass
sections.caption: the long line that connects us all
body: Amit Varma began with a poem. In Dilip Chitre’s *Father Returning Home*, a tired father gets off the train “like a word dropped from a long sentence” and falls asleep “thinking of nomads entering a subcontinent through a narrow pass.” {076-J08} That image, Varma said, is where he wanted to begin.

The first evidence of Homo sapiens, he said, is found in Africa 300,000 years ago. {#sapiens} The successful dispersal out of Africa came about 70,000 years ago; earlier migrants left no trace in the genetic record.
Between 65,000 and 60,000 years ago, some reached the subcontinent. Ajay Shah, citing Tony Joseph’s *Early Indians*, traced their route along the coast from the gulf near Basra into Kutch.

About 7,000 years ago, pastoralists from Iran settled at Mehrgarh and mingled with the early Indians; then came the Harappan civilisation. From Devdutt Pattanaik’s new book on Harappa, Varma took a frame he loves: the city’s design shows that it prioritised traders over raiders. {076-C03}
## Migration, not invasion

Around 2100 BCE came migrants from the steppes, mostly men. Talk of an Aryan invasion turned toxic, Varma said, partly because the Nazis loved the story, and partly because of a feeling that “we are the original people”.
Genetics, since Luca Cavalli-Sforza’s *The History and Geography of Human Genes*, can date such arrivals with surprising certainty. {076-R14}
~ The newcomers changed too. The Vedas, Varma said, are not one series like *Harry Potter*: the early and later Vedas are startlingly different. {076-J10}

quote.text: Ahimsa is not just nonviolence, but what is the ultimate sort of expression of it is actually peaceful trade.

sections.label: The Puranic age
sections.head: Make the dude an avatar
sections.caption: how local gods joined the family
body: As Brahmins carrying the Vedic religion fanned out across the subcontinent, Amit Varma said, they lacked the political power to impose their beliefs. So they adapted, absorbing local beliefs and telling stories about them. Those stories became the Puranas.

In Andhra, a myth had Vishnu consort with a Chenchu woman, and their child became the Chenchu god. In Tamil country, Ayyanar became Shiva’s son. Shaivites expanded Shiva’s family; Vaishnavites made a major local god an avatar. {076-S02}
Ajay Shah asked whether Hinduism stayed malleable because it was vast, oral and older than the printing press. Varma agreed: writing something down ossifies it. {076-C06}
## Rubbing shoulders

The scholar MG Ranade said Hinduism in this period was conquered by the multitudes. In Dilip Menon’s description, ancestors, local heroes, Vedic gods and nature gods “all rubbed shoulders in a seamless fabric of worship”. {076-J14}
It was no tranquil fabric. Shaivites, Vaishnavites, Jains and Buddhists destroyed each other’s places of worship; it was, Varma said, “actually like *Game of Thrones*”. {076-J09}

~ Brahmins themselves varied: some vegetarian, some not, some cremating their dead, some burying them. Hinduism, Varma said, formed from the bottom up, through the lives and rituals of people. {076-C05}

quote.text: While for Vishnu, if you’re up against a major local god, just make the dude an avatar and you’re completely fine there.

sections.label: Islam arrives
sections.head: The bandit who stayed
sections.caption: roving and stationary bandits
body: Islam first came to India not to invade but to trade, Amit Varma said, with peaceful merchants on the Kerala coast; some say within Muhammad’s lifetime. {#trade} That may be one reason communal feeling can seem lower in the south.

The raiders came from the north, and they did destroy temples. To explain what followed, Varma turned to the economist Mancur Olson. A roving bandit takes what he can and leaves nothing standing. A stationary bandit stays, and “doesn’t want to kill the goose that will lay the golden eggs”. {076-C08}

So he governs, fits in and becomes of the people, as the Mughals did by marrying Rajput princesses. Once rule settled, Varma said, citing the historian Richard Eaton, violence was confined to the edges. {076-J17}
## Mixing, and an other

Syncretism followed. In Sindh, Ali was adopted as an avatar of Vishnu. In battles between a Mughal emperor and a Hindu rebel, Varma said, half the emperor’s generals were Hindu, and Turkish mercenaries fought for Shivaji, if he remembered correctly. {076-S04}
Ajay Shah urged caution about singling out tales of cruelty, since “there are no good guys in the medieval world”. People of that period, he said, should not be judged by today’s standards.
~ Still, Varma said, for the first time there was a sense of an other to unite against. It would sharpen when colonialism began.

quote.text: you’ll find that half the generals of the Mughal Emperor were Hindu.

sections.label: The missionaries
sections.head: Ten thousand, or thirty-eight
sections.caption: colonial simplification
body: When something is too complex to grasp, Amit Varma said, the mind craves closure and makes up a story, possibly a false one. {076-C10} That is what Europeans did with an open-source religion they could not grok.
Missionaries sent back the most lurid tales they could. On sati, a real social evil, one report claimed ten thousand in a single year. When Manu Pillai checked, the figure was 38. {076-S06}

The accounts even explained sati with an incentive story built on wrong assumptions: men feared their supposedly unfaithful wives would kill them, so they made sure widows burned with them. In parts of medieval Europe, Varma noted, unfaithful wives were burnt at the stake.
## Cutting the body to fit
Once the British began to govern, they imposed their own laws. In Purushottam Agrawal’s words, “instead of cutting the cloth to fit the body, they cut the body to fit the cloth.” {076-J15}

They took a Brahminical, caste-based view of Indian religion, ran a census in which everyone ticked a box, and pushed their story through schools. To give itself a history, Varma said, quoting Sudipta Kaviraj, is a community’s most fundamental act of self-identification.
~ Unlike the early Brahmins, the colonisers wanted to rule, Varma said. Assimilation was no longer an option, and a counter-story had to be built.

quote.text: Now thirty eight is still thirty eight too many, but you know, the numbers are out of whack.

sections.label: Arriving at Hindutva
sections.head: Homeland and holy land
sections.caption: Savarkar’s test of belonging
body: From the reformers, Amit Varma said, the line runs to modern political Hinduism. His own heroes are the Congress moderates, Ranade, Gokhale and Agarkar, “men who follow liberal ends through conservative means”. {076-J18}

Gokhale was always fighting Bal Gangadhar Tilak, whom Varma finds odious in many ways: he did not want girls educated. But as a strategist he was deeply astute. He revived Shivaji as a brand and turned Ganapati, a local festival, into a grand celebration that brought hundreds of thousands onto the streets. {076-S12}
What Tilak never did was define Hinduism. That fell to Vinayak Savarkar.
## A political masterstroke

Savarkar made Hindutva the umbrella and Hinduism one part of it. To belong, India had to be both your homeland and your holy land. That othered the British, and Muslims, who turn to Mecca, while bringing in Buddhists, Jains, Shaivites, Vaishnavites and Dalits. {076-C11}

Nobody asked why the line should fall there, Varma said; it simply worked. Shruti Kapila had told him Hindutva is “a theory of violence in search of a history”. Savarkar gave it the history. {076-J16}
~ It was, Varma argued, a radical departure: a tradition that had taken in the multitudes was now built on hardcore othering.

quote.text: He realizes that if I want to build a political movement, we can’t talk about it in elite drawing rooms.

sections.label: Caste and today
sections.head: Ambedkar, meet Adam Smith
sections.caption: markets and the end of caste
body: Amit Varma took stock through caste. He often calls it Hinduism’s original sin, though it is not original as such. It is a social evil, like sati, and it has to go.

He is sceptical of top-down fixes. Savarkar insisted Dalits belonged and repeatedly held inter-caste feasts that angered Brahmins. The BJP was credited with uniting the Hindu vote in 2014; in practice it worked existing fissures like every party: non-Jatav Dalits in UP, non-Maratha OBCs in Maharashtra.

His hope lies in markets. After 1991, hundreds of millions came out of poverty, including hundreds of millions of Dalits. The Dalit scholar Chandra Bhan Prasad once told him his heroes were Ambedkar and Adam Smith. {076-S14}

Change will be slow, because paradigms change one funeral at a time. But in a free market, discrimination has a price: “A rupee is a rupee, whether a Dalit is paying you or a Brahmin is paying you.” {076-C12}
## The peak in the middle

Ajay Shah added a final force. The very poor are not especially religious, he said, and secularisation comes with wealth, education and connection to the world. The 1991 reforms put India at the religious peak of the middle. {076-C13}
~ The genteel Hinduism of Ram Mohan Roy, Tagore, Gandhi and Nehru seemed settled to Shah’s parents’ generation. Varma said it was bound to fail: “They were deracinated elites.” {076-C14}

quote.text: to be a good Hindu is perhaps to just embrace all of the world as it is and look at it with love.

side.boxText: It was his primary source for the Puranic period, Amit Varma said: Manu Pillai’s *Gods, Guns and Missionaries*, whose introductory essay, ‘A Brief History of Hinduism’, synthesises it so beautifully that everyone should go out and buy the book. {#buybook}

contQuote.text: If you want to understand your society, you have to understand the deep past. So just keep an open mind. Remember all of the things that you’re reading are description, not prescription.

p3.deck: A mouse, an ox-god, two Savarkars and a curled tongue

stories.caption: Dayanand Saraswati’s mouse
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the night that made Dayanand Saraswati
stories.head: Of mice and the Arya Samaj
body: One night at a Shiva temple, Dayanand Saraswati watched a mouse eat the prasad that had been left for the idol. As Amit Varma told it, he expected the worst: “Oh my God, this is the idol of Shiva, the God will strike the mouse down dead.” {076-S11}
Instead, “nothing happens, a mouse eats a prasad and goes away.” Dayanand began to question what he was seeing. He travelled, and spent a few years with a hermit.

He was, Varma said, a very curious man. Once, on the banks of the Ganga, he came across a corpse and cut it open: the scriptures had described what bodies look like inside, and he wanted to see if it was true. It was not.
The British were not part of his scene at all. What disgusted him was the Puranic melange, the khichdi of everything. He wanted a purer faith rooted in the early Vedas, and founded the Arya Samaj.

Yet he learned from his rivals. At the Brahmo Samaj in Kolkata, he was told he could not speak in highfalutin language; he had to speak the language of the people. {#hindi} So, Varma thinks, he began writing in Hindi.
He picked up pamphleteering, publicity, marketing and brand building there too. But he was building a different, much more militant kind of movement.

~ When Dayanand died, the elites assumed the Brahmo Samaj would thrive and the Arya Samaj would fall away. {#elites} The reverse happened. From the core of the Arya Samaj, Varma said, emerged modern political Hinduism.
stories.why: A single falsifying observation can launch a movement. Dayanand’s elite rival taught him the publicity that helped his movement outlast theirs. Real reform, Varma said, comes from below, even if it goes in directions he dislikes. {076-C14}
stories.postscript: The Brahmo Samaj became almost irrelevant outside the elite. The hosts’ dear friend Devangshu Datta is a Brahmo Samaji. {076-R21}

stories.start: The missionaries are not always in the pay of the merchants.
stories.end: only to find out it is her own lawfully wedded husband.
stories.caption: the missionaries’ tabloid tales
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on what the missionaries sent home
stories.head: The ox-god was made in Italy
body: Missionaries were not always paid by the merchants, Amit Varma said. Like a modern NGO raising funds at home, they told the most extreme version of every story. {076-S05}
One Italian missionary invented a god, half man and half ox, who demanded the blood of 400 virgins; Indian parents, in this tale, gave up children to be beheaded. {#oxgod}

Other tales were erotic. Lonely widows at the shrine of Akbar’s grandson took their pick of male pilgrims. Powerful women ran gangs that kidnapped men for a night, and one woman found her captive was “her own lawfully wedded husband”. {076-J02}
~ Europe, Varma concluded, “must have been deeply sexually repressed”. {076-J03} Voltaire read such stories and called India barbarous; James Mill wrote his history of India without visiting.
stories.why: Who pays for knowledge shapes what it says. A fundraising incentive turned reports on India into tabloid fiction, and Europe’s great thinkers built their picture of the country on it.

stories.start: the one thing that you realize is that there are two Savarkar.
stories.end: and he's completely radicalized and he just hates Muslims with a zeal.
stories.caption: the two Savarkars
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the man before and after the Andamans
stories.head: Revolutionary in, radical out
body: Amit Varma has read pretty much every biography of Vinayak Savarkar, and he sees two men. “There is a Savarkar till 1910, and there is a Savarkar that comes later.” {076-S13}

Until 1910, Savarkar was a Bhagat Singh kind of figure, Varma said, organising revolutionary acts. Nehru praised his book; he shared a stage in London with Gandhi; Hindus and Muslims, he said, must throw off the yoke together.

Then he was imprisoned in the Andamans, treated not as a political prisoner but as a terrorist. {#andamans} Between the British jailers and the prisoners stood mostly Pathan guards who brutalised the inmates; there are rumours of worse than torture.
~ He came out close to 1920 radicalised, hating Muslims with a zeal, and wrote *Essentials of Hindutva*.

quote.text: if he died in nineteen ten, we would think of him as we do of Bhagat Singh

stories.postscript: Varma has discussed Savarkar in detail with Manu Pillai on *The Seen and the Unseen*, and suggests listening to that.

stories.start: And to illustrate this, I will ask you to say the word dant.
stories.end: but you also then have this intermingling of languages.
stories.caption: Sanskrit’s borrowed sounds
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on what Sanskrit picked up from the locals
stories.head: Mothers had the last word
body: Amit Varma asked Ajay Shah to say two words. In the first, the tongue hits the upper teeth: a dental sound, common across the Indo-Aryan languages. In the second, it curls back: a retroflex sound, absent from those but present in all the Dravidian languages.

Sanskrit, arriving here, had picked these sounds up from the languages already spoken, Varma said. The point comes from Peggy Mohan’s *Wanderers, Kings, Merchants*, which cites Madhav Deshpande’s 1976 essay on the Rig Veda. {076-S01}

That essay “pretty much blew everyone away”, Varma said, because Sanskrit had been seen as pure. He had been taught that all Indian languages came from Sanskrit; that, he said, is absolutely not true.
~ Mohan’s explanation is that the migrants were mostly men who married local women. The children grew up with their mothers for their first two or three years. {#mothers}
stories.why: Even the purest sacred language is a mixture. One small fact about sounds undoes both the story of a pure origin and the story that Sanskrit is the mother of all Indian languages.

chapters.title: Intro: Not a Name, But a River
